subsubtopic: STUDIES OF FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX INCENTIVES
speechtext: Since September, 1984, has the Department of Finance conducted studies on the effects of the flow-through share tax incentives and, if so, what were the development projects studied and, in each case, what were (a) the dates of (i) commencement (/'/) completion (b) the findings of the study?

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: STUDIES OF FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX INCENTIVES
speechtext:
No, the
Department of Finance has not conducted any flow-through share studies of the nature implied in the question (i.e. studies related to specific development projects). The Department has, however, conducted other studies of flow-through shares.
In formulating advice on this issue, the Department completed a study into flow-through shares in the fall of 1984. This study examined the need for changes to the income tax legislation affecting flow-through shares.
The findings of this study provided background for the technical changes to the flow-through share legislation that were announced in the February 26, 1986 Budget. These changes eliminated the need for costly and complex private arrangements to protect the investor. The changes removed any potential liability from the investor in the event of
accidents-such as a blowout or shaft collapse-during the exploration or development program.
The recent announcement made by the Department of Finance and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the extension of the mining exploration depletion allowance (MEDA) and the introduction of the new Canadian Exploration Incentive Program (CEIP) were also the result of internal studies. These studies evaluated the rate of return and share premiums available to issuers and investors.
Other studies that provided background for the recent improvements to the flow-through share regime were a collection of submissions (both written and oral), requested by the Department of Finance, from the resource sector and the financial community. These submissions examined the flowthrough share regime after the October stock market crash. These submissions were analyzed intensively by departmental officials and provided useful information in helping to arrive at the recently announced changes to assist exploration activity.

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: FEASIBILITY OF TRANSPORTING PLUTONIUM BY AIR
speechtext:
1.	With regard to the U.S.-Japan Nuclear Co-operation Agreement to fly plutonium over a polar route, has the Government been consulted regarding emergency procedures if a landing is requested in Canadian territory and, if so (a) what is, or will be, the Government's response (b) is there a policy set out for this matter?
2.	To the knowledge of the Government, has the United States decided that plutonium will not be flown over its territory and, if so, will the Government make the same assertion?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): The U.S.A. and Japan are studying the feasibility of transporting plutonium by air on a polar route between Europe and Japan, completely outside Canadian airspace and jurisdiction. No final decisions have been taken on the route or other aspects of the flights which, in any event, are not expected to begin before the early 1990s.
During the ratification proceedings in Congress, the U.S. State Department indicated that the administration is prepared to rule out air shipments of plutonium under the Agreement from overflying or landing in the U.S.A., except in the case of an aircraft emergency. Neither the U.S.A. nor Japan has approached us regarding procedures if a landing were to be requested in Canada as a result of an aircraft emergency. However, the Government has in place procedures applicable in cases of aircraft entering Canadian airspace in an emergency. These procedures may be supplemented in any specific emergency by safety and security measures related to the nature of the cargo. While Canada has said it would not rule out flights of plutonium in advance of a specific proposal, it has also said it would most certainly prohibit such flights if not satisfied with every safety, health and security aspect thereof.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, July 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-130, an Act to implement the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Axworthy:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"this House opposes in principle and therefore declines to proceed with Bill C-130, an Act to implement the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America, because that agreement, which was negotiated in a secretive and irresponsible manner in the absence of a mandate from the Canadian people, will undermine the economic, social and political institutions of Canada, because it will fail to provide guaranteed and secure access to U.S. and other world trade markets, because it will create severe adverse effects on many industries and communities and because it will endanger the economic and social fabric and political independence of Canada".
And the amendment of Mr. Langdon:
That the amendment be amended by adding immediately after the words "political institutions of Canada," the words "including our valued system of social and regional development programs,".

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am addressing this House today because I am firmly convinced that the Free Trade Agreement is good for Canadians in general, and for Canadian women in particular.
I find it unacceptable that certain people are assuming the right to tell Canadian women that the opening of our market on the United States is a threat to their job security and to the viability of our social programs. I find that the whole free-trade debate, in fact, rests all to often on errors in perspective and inaccurate data conveyed by the Opposition.
In fact, the threat to these jobs, especially in the textile industry, comes not from the United States but from Asian countries, and these are the sectors that in the United States are most protectively fenced in by tariffs. There are plenty of Canadians active in this sector who believe they can compete effectively as long as they are given a long enough transition period, and the Accord provides for a ten-year period over which the tariffs will be amended.
Nor will there be any changes in our social programs as a whole. I will add, Madam Speaker, that I think it is dishonest and almost indecent of the Opposition to let such fears persist. We retain our sovereign right to make decisions about our social programs and our social policies. Furthermore, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) asserted at the start of the negotiations with the United-States, and I quote:
Our political sovereignty, our system of social programs, our commitment to
fight regional disparities, our unique cultural identity, our special linguistic

July 5, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
character-these are the very essence of Canada. They are not at issue in these
negotiations.
It is high time, Madam Speaker, that these so-called protectors of our national identity stopped taking women for simpletons. The Free Trade Agreement aims primarily at extending our economic, social and cultural development even further, and at building a Canada that will be even stronger and more competitive.
How can women help benefiting from the expansion of our country's economy? The Free Trade Agreement represents, for them as for all Canadians, an opportunity to improve their quality of life and increase their chances of success. Our government has already demonstrated and proven its desire to enhance the status of women in Canadian society, and it believes strongly that Canadian women must have an equal chance to contribute to our development as nation and thus to profit equally from our economic prosperity.
This desire is being translated into concrete actions. If I may, I would like to mention just a few:
-Since the Progressive Conservative Party came to power in 1984, the rate of unemployment among women has fallen by
3.6	per cent, while under the Liberals the rate climbed from
8.6	per cent to 12.0 per cent.
-Today there are 653,000 more women in the labour force than there were in 1984.
-And lastly, between 1984 and 1987, the number of women occupying professional or managerial positions increased by
36.0	per cent.
Madam Speaker, I wonder where those critics of free trade were before 1984, when the unemployment rate for women was going up by 3.4 per cent!
What our government wants is to present a blueprint for a new and progressive society, so that we can meet the challenges of the 21st century. This is why it is vitally important that we be able to progress in a stable economic climate if we want women to be represented fairly and equitably in the upper echelons of organizations, and have the same chances of succeeding professionally. And that is what the Free Trade Agreement will mean for Canada.
The Economic Council of Canada predicts that the Free Trade Agreement will result in the creation of 250,000 jobs over the next 10 years, and women, among other groups, will want access to those new jobs. An increase on this scale means that women will have greater opportunities of finding work in non-traditional sectors. In addition, 84 per cent of working women are employed in the service industries. This is the most rapidly-expanding sector of the Canadian economy. We know that free trade with the United States will mean an acceleration in our growth rate. It follows that the service sector will also experience sustained growth. This means better prospects and greater job diversity for women and for all Canadians.
Business women, who represent a significant proportion of the owners of small businesses, will also benefit from this
Agreement with the United States. For all these women, the Free Trade Agreement will make possible access to a bigger market and will safeguard trade relations between our two countries.
Among other consequences, the elimination of tariff barriers will be a direct cause of lower prices to consumers and a greater range of products, which will benefit women as it will benefit all Canadians. It is women who devote a large part of the family income to meeting essential needs such as food, shelter and clothing. It is estimated that a low-income family will be able to save up to $325 a year and that this saving could go as high as $644 a year for single women.
Madam Speaker, it is possible to frighten people. It is possible to spread false rumours. But it is not possible to deny the facts on the grounds that they don't suit our fancy. And the facts, Madam Speaker, speak for themselves.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to be taking part in this very important debate, which is going to have such serious consequences for the people of Canada. The Minister who just spoke unfortunately has raised false hopes, without any figures or data to back her up. We have seen that kind of salesmanship before. Think back to the campaign, when the Minister and all her Conservative colleagues promised a happy future for the elderly, they were going to make all kinks of progress, and the opposite happened when old-age pensions were de-indexed.
Madam Speaker, today the government is forcing us to accept a Bill, an Agreement called the Mulroney-Reagan Agreement, without really knowing what it involves.
Madam Speaker, to start with, we must bear in mind that the Prime Minister of Canada, when he was running for the leadership of his Party, came out unequivocally against a free trade deal. This is not the first time he has fooled the people, it is the n-th time. In addition, the commitments, the negotiating of an agreement with the Americans, were meant to remove any possibility of the American government's taking reprisals against the Canadian government. Think back to the soft-wood lumber affair. Up to that point it was an excellent idea to make sure, to enable our Quebecois and Canadian enterprises to sell their products on the American market, but first of all there were conditions that the Liberal Party and our leader called for: Canadian sovereignty, the fact of being "maitres chez nous" as we call it in Quebec, had to be protected; second, culture could not be negotiable; third, nothing about our social programs could be affected, they could not be negotiable, they must not be "put on the table"; and fourth, agriculture also had to be completely protected, it could not be negotiated.
Unfortunately, we all know what happened, and as the Coalition du Quebec, which is made up of the Union des producteurs agricoles [Quebec farmers' federation] and the federated unions, has demonstrated, the result is that the
July 5, 1988

Prime Minister of Canada gave the President of the United States a horse and got a rabbit in exchange. That is what the government wants us to approve today. And why do I have reservations about accepting such an agreement? Because the Minister of Transport himself (Mr. Bouchard), who was Minister of Employment and Immigration at the time, the MP for Roberval himself said that according to studies carried out by this Department, as many as 500,000 jobs could be lost. And I have here figures from a study by the Economic Council, which is an organization that approves of the idea of free trade, and these figures-contrary to what the Minister has just said-show clearly that there will be jobs lost in the textile industry, in the footwear industry, in the clothing industry, in the electricity, cables and wires industry, in a number of industries, and in agriculture.
Madam Speaker, we know there will be losers, we know there will be winners. I know in advance that Bernard Lamarre is going to be a millionaire four times over with Lavalin. I'm not worried about him and he has no need of the House of Commons. His shareholders are going to be better off too, that's certain. But one thing I don't know, and nobody can guarantee it, not even Bernard Lamarre of Lavalin: who can put down in black and white a guarantee that their employees are going to be better paid, and that there are going to be more men and women in Quebec, in all of Canada, with jobs? Mr. Lamarre can't guarantee that. My friend Lortie of Provigo, is also in favor of the deal. He's sure his shareholders are going to be better off. But there again he can't guarantee in black and white that there are going to be more jobs in Provigo and Provigain stores opened in Quebec. He won't sign a piece of paper saying that those new stores won't be opened in Plattsburgh-that a new Provigo will provide jobs for the people of Plattsburgh. Madam
Speaker, a few days ago hundreds of thousands of Canadians celebrated Canada Day, Canada's birthday, with a feeling of pride in the accomplishments of our country over the past 121 years. There was a great deal of celebration and a great deal of jubilation. I suspect that the celebration on July 1, Canada's birthday, may be the last celebration of its kind that we will experience in Canada because the Bill we are debating today, C-130, should really be called "The Turning of Canada into the 51st American State".
We have spent 121 years building our country into one that is unique in the world, one that reflects ideals and values which are admired by people from all countries. We have built a society here distinct from that of the United States. After 121 years of building, the Conservative Government, in only three years, has sold it out to the highest bidder, in this case the United States of America.
What we have seen in this country over the last three years under the Conservative Government can only be described as anti-Canadian activity. There is no question that we have lost our sovereignty as a nation because of this trade deal. A lot of people have said that we have sold out the country. When you sell something it is assumed that you get something in return. This was a give-away of Canada for all intents and purposes to the United States.
Not only is this legislation anti-Canadian, it is also antidemocratic. You will recall yourself, Madam Speaker, as I am sure many Members will, that just prior to the last general election when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was asked whether he supported a free trade deal, he said that he was against a free trade deal with the United States. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was asked whether he supported a free trade deal with the United States and he said that he was against a free trade deal with the United States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) was asked whether he supported a trade deal with the United States and he said that he was against a trade deal of this kind with the United States.
I could name a number of other senior cabinet Ministers who, when asked that question, said that they opposed a free trade deal with the United States. The people of Canada assumed that the Prime Minister and some of his most powerful cabinet Ministers, having said that they were against a free trade deal with the United States, were against a free
trade deal with the United States. All that we as citizens can do is believe that what the Prime Minister says is the truth.
We then had a general election, and not one single time during the federal election campaign in 1984 was free trade even mentioned. Not once did free trade with the United States come up for discussion or debate by the Prime Minister or anyone else in the Conservative Party anywhere in Canada. Then, on January 2, 1988, the Prime Minister signed a deal with the United States called a free trade deal.
This, then, is undemocratic because the Government misled the people of Canada. I think it is fair to say that those people were dishonest when they said that they were against free trade. They did not even mention it in the campaign and then, after being elected, are going to lock Canada into this deal, sell out the country forever, and turn Canada into the fifty-first state of the United States. The Prime Minister can be the governor of the "Estate of Canada".
This is also unparliamentary. After months and months of intensive negotiations in secret by various negotiators, the Prime Minister, and some of his major advisers, the Parliament of Canada has been given five days to debate this issue. As you well know, Madam Speaker, we sometimes spend four or five days on a fairly simple tax Bill which will amend the Income Tax Act.
This, however, is not a typical piece of legislation. In the Prime Minister's words, this is the most important trade legislation in the world. The Prime Minister has said that it is the most important trade deal ever struck between two nations and he has allocated only five days for parliamentary debate. The Government is now going to use its huge majority to curtail debate, muzzle Parliament, and for all intents and purposes prevent it from working effectively on behalf of the people of Canada.
Not only is this legislation anti-Canadian and anti-democratic, it is also anti-parliamentary. I could add that it is also anti-constitutional. One of the key components of this trade deal is the paragraph which says that this deal overrides all provincial legislation. It does not matter whether this deal goes against the Constitution of Canada or the negotiations which the federal Government has had with provincial Governments over the last 121 years, this deal takes precedence. When push comes to shove we can forget all the arrangements that we have made constitutionally and through negotiations with the provinces. That is clearly unconstitutional.
It is preposterous when you think that this deal is about to be wrapped up through closure when you consider what the deal does for us. Canada set out to accomplish three basic things. One was open, guaranteed, and secure access to the American market. Time and again the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) indicated that if we did not get unrestricted access to the huge American market of 242 million, there would be no deal. We did not get unrestricted
July 5, 1988

access to the American market. The United States administration retains the right to launch countervail and anti-dumping suits against Canada.
In other words, nothing has changed. The situation between Canada and the United States as a result of this deal will be the same next year as it was 10 years ago. The Americans retain the right to launch countervail against Canada as they did on softwood lumber, shakes and shingles, steel, and in other areas. Therefore we failed to achieve that ultimate goal we had set out.
Second, we wanted a binding dispute settlement mechanism so that if there was a dispute between Canada and the United States in terms of trade in a certain commodity, there would be a powerful decision-making body with teeth which could move in quickly and resolve the dispute. We failed to accomplish our second bottom line. All we got was a review panel to ensure that the Canadians and Americans are following the laws of their countries in a trade dispute. This panel has no teeth, it has no ability to move in and make a quick decision. Therefore, we failed to achieve our second bottom line as well.
Finally, we wanted an exemption against the United States protectionist trade laws. We did not get that either. The Americans retained the right to pass what they call trade remedy legislation against Canada and we accepted that. Therefore, we failed to achieve every single one of the three fundamentals which we set out to obtain.
The Americans also had three fundamentals which they hoped to achieve and they got all three of them. First, they wanted unlimited access to our markets. They wanted to be able to move in and buy immediately a company valued under $150 million. The Government gave them that right. The Government said that the Americans can have secure access to our energy resources and we cannot charge them more than we are charging our own customers. Third, they wanted to harmonize the wage laws, workplace laws, pension systems, and so on of the two countries. Canadians do not want the Americans to have any of those three objectives.
I am afraid my time is up, Madam Speaker. I hope I will have a chance to return to this another time.

We have quite broad support in the agriculture sector, although I concede that there are still some concerns there.

In fact, I am thoroughly convinced that as a precondition to any negotiations opening up on free trade, the United States President demanded that Canada amend its Patent Act. There is absolutely no question about that, and that is indeed what happened.
Canada did amend its Patent Act and that legislation went through the House last year. During the debate on amendments to the Patent Act, seniors across Canada predicted that if the amendments the Government was trying to ram through the House and indeed did ram through the House at that time became law, drug prices would return to what they were prior to 1969 when the drug companies enjoyed a monopoly on drug prices in Canada. The Government, and particularly the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), denied that that would happen and continues to deny that that has been happening. Yet we know that since that legislation went through the House, many drug prices have increased by some 50 per cent over what they were a year ago.
We also know that shortly after the Shamrock Summit at which social programs were probably discussed, the first Budget was presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), containing a proposal to deindex old age pensions. That may be a coincidence, but I doubt it very much. In line with the proposal to deindex pensions which senior citizens fought against and forced the Government to back off on, the Government also proposed and still proposes to deindex public service pensions. In my view, that is the opening round of the attack against the pension system.
On top of that, since this Government was elected, it has opened up the medicare system to private enterprise in the United States. Our hospitals are now open to the American style of administration which is medicare for profit, a thing that Canadians have fought against since Tommy Douglas introduced the first medicare program in Saskatchewan. Medicare is a valued program in Canada.
When Canadian seniors go to Florida and see what happens to our American neighbours when they run into medical difficulties and find out how much it costs them for medical services, and then look at what the Government has been doing in terms of opening up the medicare system to multinational organizations which operate it for profit, they become concerned. I do not blame them for becoming concerned, because I can very well visualize that some time within the next seven-year period, this Government, if it is still in power, will open up the whole area of social policy in the free trade negotiations. I hope this Government will not be around after the next election so that it cannot follow that kind of course, but there is absolutely no doubt in my mind whatsoever that the steps taken since 1984 until this time have been a direct attack on Canada's social programs. I think it will be made even worse after this trade agreement is signed on January 1 of next year.
I expected some Conservative Members to start taking umbrage to what I have been saying.

subtopic: ELEVATION TO CARDINALATE OF MONSEIGNEUR PAUL GREGOIRE
ELEVATION TO CARDINALATE OF MONSEIGNEUR PAUL GREGOIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday, in Rome, a Canadian parliamentary delegation of which I was a member witnessed the elevation of Msgr. Paul Gregoire, Archbishop of Montreal, to the cardinalate.
This most impressive religious ceremony was graced by the presence and imposing personality of His Holyness John-Paul II, of course, but all of the delegates from some eighty nations also had the opportunity of noting at first hand the simplicity and moral stature that radiate from the personable Cardinal His Eminence Msgr. Gregoire of Montreal.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED GOLF COURSE ON VANCOUVER
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED GOLF COURSE ON VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has before it a proposal to build a golf course at Royal Roads Military College at Colwood, Vancouver Island. Local people object to the proposal for a number of reasons. First, the golf course would eliminate an attractive area of bush with several large trees. This would
aggravate an already serious problem with surface water at a nearby subdivision.
Most seriously, however the proposed golf course threatens the Esquimau Lagoon. Golf courses use large quantities of chemical fertilizer to maintain the greens. At Royal Roads much of this would drain into Esquimau Lagoon.
One biologist wrote me to say that the influx of nutrients would stimulate rapid growth of unicellular plants and a tremendous production of biomass. When that died and decomposed it would rob the water of oxygen. Fish and invertebrates would die from lack of oxygen and birds would no longer land. The lagoon would begin to stink. Instead of being a place of life and beauty, it would have been destroyed.
We are only beginning to recognize the importance of lagoons, salt marshes, and estuaries in the total ecology of our world. Since the proposed golf course poses a real threat to the Esquimalt Lagoon I urge the Government not to consent to its construction.

subtopic: RIGHT TO LIFE UPHELD
RIGHT TO LIFE UPHELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian society today does not, and I hope it never will, permit a doctor, or two doctors, or Parliament, or anyone else to choose whether a crippled senior riddled with disease should live or be murdered. He has a right to live. Why, then, should one or two doctors, or Parliament, or anyone else decide whether an unborn human baby should live or be murdered?
The motion and both amendments concerning this matter presently on the Order Paper permit a choice. Who gave us the right to choose? I cannot support the motion or the amendments. Human life is fundamental to our society. The right to live is not negotiable. That is why I support Bill S-16 which protects human life from the moment of conception. The choice is God's, not ours.

subtopic: CONDITION OF MEAFORD, ONT., HARBOUR
CONDITION OF MEAFORD, ONT., HARBOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the condition of two harbours in Meaford, Ontario, located on Georgian Bay, was recently brought to my attention.
Last August the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) announced a plan to build a new harbour. This project was to be fully completed within the next two years. This year a drastic drop in water levels rendered the existing harbour
July 5, 1988

unusable. In fact, the Coast Guard had to relocate its vessel to Owen Sound.
Despite numerous requests the federal Government refused to dredge the harbour which was last dredged 26 years ago.
In a letter dated April 22, 1988, the Minister said: It is anticipated that the present water levels will increase by one foot by the beginning of May. This will help reduce the quantity of dredging required to have the harbour at least partially operational for the summer of 1988." The water level has not changed and finally, after a loud protest, the Minister came up with $50,000 for emergency dredging but local citizens would have to match it.
I believe that providing and maintaining safe harbours is a responsibility which deserves proper funding from the federal treasury. To make matters worse, departmental officials have advised local citizens that they will also be responsible for any dredging in the new harbour.
I call on the Government to allocate the necessary funds to ensure that Canadians in Meaford and across this country will have safe harbours.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN REALITY
THE CANADIAN REALITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in July 1969, the federal Government officially recognized that Canada was a bilingual country. From 1969 to 1984, a period of almost fifteen years but for a few months, the Liberal Government did not, during all those years it was in power, do a single thing to promote the French fact in Canada. And today, the federal Liberals have the gall to criticize us! Even if there were a few amendments, Mr. Speaker, we would still have more to be proud of than the idleness the Liberal Governmment indulged in during those fifteen years. Bilingualism is a Canadian reality, and we are going to do everything in our power to make Francophones and Anglophones feel at home everywhere in Canada, in a stronger and more united Canada.

subtopic: B.C. LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS WEEKLY REPORT-REQUEST FOR SECOND-CLASS MAILING STATUS
B.C. LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS WEEKLY REPORT-REQUEST FOR SECOND-CLASS MAILING STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the British Columbia Livestock Producers Co-Operative
Association publishes a weekly market report for its 2,200 members. This publication is devoted exclusively to agriculture and provides practical and essential information for British Columbia cattlemen to enable them to make well informed decisions about livestock production.
The severe drought conditions, coupled with increasing insecurity due to international and domestic market fluctuations, increasing feed costs, unfair competitive practices, and many other challenges, make it mandatory for cattlemen to have all the pertinent information possible to deal effectively and efficiently in today's market-place.
The Association requested second-class mailing status for its informative publication but the request was rejected by Canada Post. Second-class mail status would save the cooperative thousands of dollars in mailing costs. As well, by granting this request Canada Post would add considerably to the viability and stability of the British Columbia livestock industry.
I appeal to the Minister responsible for Canada Post and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to do whatever is necessary to enable the British Columbia Livestock Producers CoOperative Association to receive second-class mailing status for this market publication.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT IN NORTH SYDNEY, N.S.
EMPLOYMENT IN NORTH SYDNEY, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 20 the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) said that the closure of the railroad in Newfoundland would not mean any job losses in North Sydney. This was confirmed to him by both Canadian National and Marine Atlantic. Yet the very next day, June 21, CN sent a directive to all its offices in Atlantic Canada directing them to send all containers for eastern Newfoundland east of Gander, including St. John's and all of the Avalon Peninsula, to Halifax for shipment directly to St. John's.
The President of Atlantic Container Express has said that the closure of the Newfoundland railroad will mean an increase in cargo shipments from Montreal to Corner Brook and St. John's of 12 to 15 per cent in 1988.
While the people in Montreal are counting new jobs the Government refuses to acknowledge the loss of jobs in North Sydney. Why is this happening? Why is the Government refusing to give compensation to the town and the people of North Sydney? Why is the Government doing unofficially what it refused to do officially, that is, acknowledge the loss of traffic in North Sydney, which is perhaps a prelude to the closure of the railroad in Nova Scotia between Truro and North Sydney?

EFFECT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS ON MANITOBA TEACHERS' PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I had occasion to meet with representatives of the Manitoba Teachers' Society to hear their concerns about draft amendments to the Income Tax Act and the effect that some of these will have on the early retirement provisions of their pension plan. It is a concern shared by other groups as well, such as the Manitoba Organization of Nurses Associations.
For example, the teachers' plan has, over the years, been bargained from a point of full actuarial reduction between age 55 and 60 to a point where this was eliminated entirely in 1985 with a service requirement of only 10 years.
The Government's proposals would set this progress back 20 years and unilaterally undo an important dimension of a benefits package that was arrived at through teachers giving up other things at the bargaining table because of their conviction about the importance of full early retirement benefits in a stress-filled profession which also has many younger teachers unable to find work. At a penalty of 3 per cent a year, which the Government proposes, a 15 per cent reduction for those retiring at age 55 is almost certain to prohibit such needed retirements and the consequent turnovers.
Furthermore, the proposal to lengthen service requirements discriminates against women, many of whom have had to interrupt their careers. Teachers and health care workers in particular are concerned about these proposals as both groups have a very high proportion of women. I call on the Government to rethink these ill thought out proposals.

IMPACT OF PROPOSED PAROLE CENTRE ON YORK-SOUTH WESTON
speechtext:

The committee has examined ways in which Canada could play a constructive and positive role. Clearly, the peace process itself must continue to be directed by Central Americans. Canada's role should be to assist and to encourage those in charge of that process.
Specifically, Canada can immediately help in designing and possibly participating in ceasefire verification systems. In fact, we are awaiting a formal invitation. Beyond that, Canada can strengthen the peace process through human rights and democratic development programs, economic assistance and by the consolidation of diplomatic representation in the region.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this debate that we are currently involved in is about two possible futures for our country. The one possibility is based clearly and constructively on our own historical traditions and the other represents a clear departure from that tradition and a radical shift away from what has become the Canadian heritage.
Beyond the surface similarities, there are on this North American continent of ours two strongly competing images of the good life. If this deal is consummated, the odds are very great that it will be at once witness and participant to the triumph of one image over the other.
With unintended irony, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in his first speech in the House of Commons: "Give us 20 years and you will not recognize this country". Well, we do not intend to give the Prime Minister 20 years. We do not intend to give him even eight years because we love this country of ours, and it is neither desirable nor his right to change our country beyond recognition.

Madam Speaker, this agreement surrenders our inalienable right to make our own decisions. It takes away our right to control our ancestral heritage. It denies us control over our natural resources. It even makes our water available to the United States. It threatens many jobs in our factories, in the agricultural sector and in our resource industries. It is a threat to the Auto Pact. It is a threat to women, especially those working in the service industries. It weakens our control over the environment. It gives Washington powers that are the prerogative of our provincial capitals. Madam Speaker, it does not even guarantee us access to the U.S. market. This agreement is totally unacceptable.
Although it does all these things, and for those reasons alone, in the opinion of my colleagues and a majority of Canadians who have now become more and more familiar with what is involved, the deal should be rejected. Today I want to talk about the much broader context within which I believe this accord ought to be seen. I do this because I deeply believe that what is at risk is the very idea of Canada as it has come to be known, particularly during the last five decades.

I may point out, Madam Speaker, that I did not say Canada itself is at risk. What is at risk is our present values, those that are shared and respected by all Canadians, both Francophones and Anglophones. If we hold these values dearly, we cannot accept this agreement. I am not talking about economics but about values and principles.
July 5, 1988



This debate is not about whether one narrowly defined economic system or aspect of commercial activity or another should be accepted. That is a much too restrictive interpretation to put on what is clearly involved in this historic decision. This debate is really about whether what I would call the Canadian way or the American way will prevail in our country. Both images overlap, of course, but such commonality should not obscure some very important and quite profound differences.
If you will permit me, I would first like to explain what I mean when I say "The American way". I mean by that a kind of society in which not only market values have been embedded in the system directly, but one in which those values come to dominate virtually every aspect of life. I want to be specific. I refer not simply to the buying of goods and services according to market principles but to the virtual transformation of everything else in society within the framework of those market values. I refer to culture, I refer to religion, I refer to social policy-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Religion?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
-all of which, I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), properly understood in American society, have come to be dominated by market values. The most significant growth in religion, I say to the Minister, is in the fundamentalist sects in the U.S. which have come to equate Christianity with the successful making of money. That is not my view, it is a view which has been expressed not only by some North American but the world's leading theologians.
Market values have come to be all pervasive in the United States. Of course, and I say it right away, there are exceptions, but this is unquestionably the pattern of U.S. development as every serious observer from Alexis de Tocqueville in the past to Michael Harrington in the present has had the intelligence and insight to understand. It has its pluses and it has its minuses, but Canada has marched to the tune of a different drummer.
Yes, we, too, have accepted the market principle in Canada but from the very outset of our country's history we understood the limitations that ought to be put on that system. We have not allowed market values to become all pervasive. We are committed to life and liberty but we are also committed to a sense of community. This has become in my view particularly marked during the historical developments of the last 50 years but also, as I said, right at the outset.
Our founding Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, well understood that if this country called Canada, with its two founding nations but soon to be rich and diverse in language and cultures, was to survive, then something other than market values would have to exist. That was particularly true at that time as illustrated by state involvement in the building of our transportation system, which would never have come into being if we had relied upon the market system of the United States.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
However, as I say, the changes which have come to characterize and distinguish Canadian life from American life have become most marked since the 1930s and, I would argue, have now come to be so pervasive that it makes immense good sense to talk about a Canada distinctively different from the country immediately to the south. It is in this development we have taken on a character as a nation that makes us much more similar to countries in the northern part of Europe than to the United States of America.
Recently, to illustrate a small point, I was invited to speak in another country. I left my home, got in my car, bought gas in a PetroCan gas station, listened to the CBC, and got on an Air Canada plane. All of this was perfectly routine for me. All of those institutions, as Canadians will recognize, are Canadian institutions in the public sector, none of which exist in those forms in the U.S.
Let me be even more concrete in talking about how different values have worked themselves out in our two quite different nations. First, something which is on the surface mundane and practical, is our medicare system. In the U.S., because of a different value system, the medical care system is still regarded as a marketable item to be bought and sold in the market-place like any other good or service. Americans are encouraged to fend for themselves. The consequence, of course, has been that in the U.S. today there are 36 million Americans without any form of medical insurance whatsoever, twelve million of whom happen to be children. In Canada, where we made the decision that the market-place is not something to dictate all values, we took medical services out of the marketplace and have long since regarded them as a right of citizenship, not simply a good to be purchased by whoever can afford it.
If we look again at something as practical in the lives of real human beings as unemployment insurance and minimum wages, we find once again the value systems of the two countries are quite different. In the U.S. there is a strong belief that if a man or woman becomes unemployed, it is predominantly to be understood to be his or her own fault. In Canada we recognize, particularly since the 1930s, in our institutions reflecting the change in values, that if a man or a woman becomes unemployed, overwhelmingly the fault is not within that man or woman but in the economic system. As a consequence of these two quite different value systems the two countries have assumed quite different practical institutions. In the U.S. today only 25 per cent of American workers are covered by unemployment insurance. In Canada, 85 per cent of workers are covered by unemployment insurance. In Canada, all provincial minimum wages are over $3.20 an hour. Eight states in the U.S. have absolutely no minimum wage whatsoever and three are set at less than $1.60 an hour.
Another practical aspect is the right of trade unions, to which people on the other side very frequently allude when talking about countries like Poland. They claim the importance

July 5, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
of trade unions in that country and other unfree systems but are only very infrequently prepared to defend those institutions here in Canada. I, as a Canadian, believe that apart from the development of democracy itself in the last 100 years, the right of trade unions to exist in developed societies is probably the most important institution giving freedom to workers which has emerged in the last 100 years.
In Canada our rate is hardly yet comparable to western and northern Europe, but 37 per cent of our workforce is in unions. However, in the United States only 17 per cent of the workforce is unionized. While the situation continually gets better in our country, I regret to say that it continually gets worse in the United States.
With regard to agriculture, when subsidies have been brought to bear in the United States, they have been seen to be anomalous to the system and described as exceptions to the rule. They have been said to be temporary even if they have lasted, at times, a decade or so. In other words, they have gone against the prevailing system which is to leave each farmer on his own, not only in the market-place in the United States but in the global market-place.
In Canada our approach has been different once again. With regard to institutions as diverse as the Canadian Wheat Board and marketing boards for egg, poultry, and milk producers, we have not responded simply in an ad hoc fashion to bail farmers out in any given crisis. We have seen farmers and farming families as an integral part of the community with rights which should include certain organizational principles which will not leave them the uncared for victims of a market system which can simply throw them hither or yon. Once again, we have brought an organizational principle to the economy which differs radically from that which exists in the United States.
Another area is regional development. We in this country have developed, particularly since the Great Depression, a commitment to the view that regional development is fundamental to the notion of what Canada is all about. Some of us worked hard in the 1981-82 constitutional period to ensure that the notion of equality was written into our Constitution in terms of regional development opportunities. I can tell you that you will not find that in the United States Constitution where, once again, the concept of a market-place prevails.
I go beyond my Party on everything I have said in terms of value systems. Elements in all Parties and all regions believe that a young boy or girl growing up in this country in 1988 ought not to have to move to Toronto to get a job. Our diverse country has really four or five economies within the bosom of one nation. We believe that the federal Government has a fundamental obligation to deal with regional economic development. In our view the present Government has not adequately addressed that issue.
The principle I am talking about is crucial. We have become aware as a nation of the importance of that principle in our economic development whereas in the United States, apart
from the crisis actions of Roosevelt in the 1930s with the Tennessee Valley Authority, the only major economic policy coming from the national government in terms of regional economic development has been to use the military as an instrument for building jobs in one part of the country or another. The notion that you ought to interfere within the so-called natural workings of the market-place to ensure genuine equality of opportunity and development is not embedded in the philosophical system of that country.

Similarly, in cultural policy, our country, again in a tradition much closer to that of Europe, and many Asiatic countries as well, has almost from the start had the view that the Government as well as individual citizens outside the state mechanism have an important role to play in culture. Whether talking about the CBC, regulations in broadcasting policy to ensure Canadian content, provincial and federal Government grants for major art projects, or tax laws designed to encourage the development of Canadian magazines and the fostering of Canadian publishers, we have seen a role of the democratic state in the encouragement and fostering of Canadian individual talent. That tradition, shared elsewhere in the world, has been profoundly absent in the United States.
I want to make the point that important value differences exist which distinguish us from the United States. We have very different approaches to medicare, unemployment insurance, unions, farmers, regional development, wage policy, and culture. In short, Canadian life is remarkably different and, I believe, remarkably better in these crucial aspects of existence than in the United States.

I want to talk about our programs and how confident we are that they will be able to meet the adjustment needs caused by free trade. As I have outlined, adjustment is part of a healthy and growing economy. But to ensure the fastest and most relevant response to change and to opportunity, to ensure that Canadians can take advantage of opportunity, the Government has an established advisory council on adjustment. That council consists of representatives from business and labour and consumer groups and educational institutions, with ex officio representation from the Government. It will assess our programs to make sure that existing programs are being used effectively and, also, to ensure that we keep ahead of emerging opportunities in the labour market, because opportunities are such an important part of adjustment.
Let me end where I began. For Canadian women, free trade will mean new opportunities for employment and new opportunities for advancement in their service careers, in the manufacturing sector and in their farming and entrepreneurial lives.
Free trade-and this is where it catches the imagination- presents Canada and Canadians with both challenges and opportunities. It challenges the status quo, slow growth and limited opportunity and restricted expectations, all of which have hampered women's chances of fulfilling their potential in a country that is bursting with promise.

Free trade also offers Canada opportunities to broaden our economic and industrial capabilities as a nation and to expand the employment choices in the manoeuvrability of our workforce. This will surely benefit women, who represent a major source of our nation's potential for future jobs and, as I said in the beginning, who are full contributors as entrepreneurs, as consumers, and as workers.
New opportunity is what this agreement is about, for our regions, our industrial sectors, for individual Canadians, for men and for women and, most particularly, for our children and for our grandchildren who are going to look at the opportunities that we have left them, who are going to look at how they can afford the social programs that we have today, who are going to look at the history of our country, which began with traders and has continued with traders. Whenever we have expanded our trade potential, our opportunities have increased. We owe our children and our grandchildren no small legacy. What we owe them is the opportunities that we have had over the past 40 years and will continue to have through the expansion of our trade opportunities.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is probably fair to say that no one can predict with any accuracy or any great certainty either the economic effects or the impact of this Canada-U.S. trade deal. I think the Government's propaganda that this will open the door to unprecedented future prosperity, that it will be the panacea for all of our future economic woes, has to be overstating the case, must be challenged and can be challenged.
The Hon. Mitchell Sharp, himself a former Trade and Commerce Minister, as well as Minister of Finance and Minister of External Affairs, a gentleman who served with great distinction in this House and was respected by all, has written recently, and I believe written objectively, the following:
It is difficult to contest the assertion, at least theoretically, that the removal of remaining trade barriers between Canada and the United States would, after time-perhaps a difficult time-result in a net economic benefit to both countries, and that Canada would share this benefit, which would however be relatively modest.
So I would like to refer to three aspects of the agreement that are involved in Bill C-130. First of all, those remaining trade barriers, second, the difficult times which this agreement will undoubtedly bring for some and perhaps for many; and finally, the benefits and the costs of this agreement to our Canadian nation.
First of all, let me say that the Canadian resource sector seems generally to favour the trade agreement. They do so mainly because they believe that this agreement will provide them with a secure access to an ever expanding U.S. market. I think the question for Hon. Members is: Will it? The forest products industry has already paid heavily for this agreement in the form of a 15 per cent export tax or, now translated in some parts of Canada into higher stumpage fees, additional

July 5, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
government costs imposed upon the industry. The forest products industry paid dearly and paid heavily. They did so because Canadian lumber prior to the last countervail action was taking a larger share of the U.S. market. They were doing so as a result of our Canadian industry being more efficient and competitive, coupled with the advantage that we had from a favourable exchange rate.
Michael B. Percy and Christian Yoder, in an outstanding piece of work, a study of the softwood lumber dispute, concluded:
It is clear that once a Canadian industry increases its market share in the United States, the formidable array of contingent-protection mechanisms will be brought to bear on it.
And he said:
Canadian industries are thus very aware that continued access to the U.S. markets depends critically on not exceeding some implicit or explicit market share.
I contend and I say to you, Madam Speaker, and to all Hon. Members, that this principle was in effect before the trade agreement was negotiated and signed, before Bill C-130, and this principle will be in effect after Bill C-130 and the trade agreement go into effect. Surely, everyone of us in this House can understand that for any beleaguered U.S. industry all competition tends to be unfair and injurious, even if that competition stems from true market-based cost advantage. That is a thesis that has been tested in the past and will be tested in the future.
Market share, I predict, will continue to be a problem for Canadian industries selling into the United States of America. At the same time, the pricing of our resources will in many cases cease to be under our control. If a province, for example, were to restrict production of a particular resource in order to raise the export price of that resource, the province could very well be faced with a challenge under the agreement we are ratifying today. Thus, on the one hand, our access to U.S. markets will continue to be restricted and will continue to be a problem for many Canadian industries and on the other hand, U.S. access to our resources at the best possible price for them will be assured. That being the case, Madam Speaker, is it any wonder that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) when he was Minister of Energy in 1979 told Jack McArthur of the Toronto Star.
Free trade in energy with the Americans is like wife swapping with a bachelor.
Second, while I acknowledge that there may be a modest economic gain for Canada after a period of time, perhaps a time of some difficulty, what can be said of these difficulties which are almost certainly to be encountered by a large number of workers in this country? What can we say about these times of trouble? During the adjustment period I asked what help would be available for displaced workers. I tried to listen with great care to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall). She tried to leave the
impression in this House that the existing programs, labour adjustment and job strategy will be enough. I would like to challenge her and all members on the government side and say to them that 1 doubt that very much.
The Government of Canada has not tied this comprehensive trade agreement to a comprehensive adjustment program for industries that will be adversely affected, for employees that will be displaced or for the communities in which they live to be assisted.
1 want to tell you, Madam Speaker, that I do not share the total faith of this Government or the faith of President Reagan or Mrs. Thatcher, a total faith in the intrinsic value of unrestricted, unfettered free market forces. Of course, it is true that they create enormous wealth for some. Undoubtedly that is the case, but at the same time it also imposes terrible poverty and tragic hardship on others, and we can expect to see more of that in Canada as a result of this Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
Finally, what will it cost Canada to embrace this policy of continentalism, which is implicit in Bill C-130? Sir Robert Borden said in an election message to Canadians in 1911:
We must decide whether the spirit of Canadianism or if continentalism shall prevail in the northern half of this continent.
That message won for Mr. Borden an election in that year. Again, I refer to the analysis offered by Mr. Mitchell Sharp. He told us it is difficult to determine with accuracy the economic benefits. He went on to say:
It is equally difficult to contest the assertion that a comprehensive preferential trade agreement with the United States would to some extent at least erode Canadian independence and sense of identity.
W. L. Mackenzie King is quoted as having said in 1948:
I felt sure that the long objective of the Americans was to control this continent. They would want to get Canada under their aegis.
In his diary in 1950 he wrote:
The more I think over the whole situation, the more I believe... that the U.S. foreign policy at bottom is to bring Canada into as many situations affecting themselves as possible with a view to leading ultimately to the annexation of our two countries.
Despite Mrs. Thatcher's purring assurances in this House that national identity is not at stake in comprehensive trade agreements, I do fear that a large, powerful, rich and influential nation like the United States of America can easily overwhelm us if we let it happen. I believe that Bill C-130 and this trade deal will help make that possible.
There is an old Indian elder in my constituency who lives along the shores of James Bay. I consider him to be one of the wisest gentlemen with whom I have ever had the privilege of conversing. He said to me not long ago when we were speaking about this trade agreement with the United States, and I end on this:
Beware, when a small nation makes a treaty with a large and powerful one-look what happened to us.
July 5, 1988

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am interested in participating in the debate on Bill C-130. I would like to spend another moment or two tracking the history or, as I have said before, tracking the genetics of this deal.
It was not a proposal that swelled from northwestern British Columbia or from British Columbia or from any of the provinces or either of the territories or from any single identifiable group within Canada; it is a business deal that was hatched in the late 1970s in the United States and became part of the campaign platform of Ronald Reagan. It took a number of years for the Republicans to find someone who could carry it forward in Canada but they certainly found a willing person in the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney).
Prior to being elected in 1983-84 he went on the record time and again openly opposing the concept of a trade deal with the United States. I suppose if one looks back at the track record of the present Prime Minister of Canada, one can see perhaps, in his handling of Schefferville, how the Iron Ore Company used him as a proxy for the United States to close down that community and to close up Schefferville and turn it into a ghost town. Perhaps going back even earlier to his childhood, one finds that he used to sit on the knees of visiting American dignitaries and, for a couple of bucks, sing Danny Boy.
We should look too at the present Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie). As I said yesterday evening, it was that same Crosbie family who wore black arm bands in 1949. They were so discouraged that Newfoundland would join Canada and Confederation rather than becoming part of the United States, that they thought it was something to mourn over.
There are a certain number of tests to which one must put any piece of legislation in order to determine whether or not it is worthy of a nation's approval. I suppose one would have to start by asking if the deal is reciprocal, does Canada get as good a deal based on a careful reading of the text as the United States does. The answer, of course, is clearly no.
The principle that was enunciated time and time again by government Members across the country as being the absolute bottom line was that unless there was a binding dispute settlement mechanism, the deal could not fly, the negotiations would have to be called off. Anyone would know after taking a look at the agreement that there is no binding dispute mechanism in it because U.S. law prevails under all circumstances.
Bill C-130 places all Acts of this legislature, all Acts of Parliament, beneath it. It places all Acts of the legislatures of the provinces and territories subsidiary to it, but it is not the same situation on the U.S. side. Bill C-130 places everything below it in Canada. It rises above all other Acts. However, in the United States, of course it is U.S. trade law that will prevail.
Let us take a moment to contrast our two nations, the two systems, and see where this deal is likely to go. Let us begin
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
with a point of evaluation made by the present Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher). While he was holding another portfolio, he calculated that the dislocation in the labour market will affect about 800,000 workers in the short term. The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), while he was the Minister of Employment and Immigration, estimated that up to 500,000 Canadians could lose their jobs because of the trade deal. Those are not figures that came from the NDP research department or figures that I saw written on the back of the curtains somewhere. Those are figures developed by the Government of Canada for the Conservatives to be used publicly.
Let us look at the binding dispute settlement mechanism. Binational panels are bound only to U.S. laws and practices whenever U.S. firms want to challenge how we do things in Canada. They have no powers to investigate, gather facts or direct national agencies to make specific judgments. All they can do is to judge whether American trade legislation has been applied properly.
Governed by U.S. law and precedent, the U.S. can define subsidies almost any way it wants to. It can continue to harass Canadian exporters and block free access over such issues as research and development grants, seasonally-adjusted unemployment insurance and regional-provincial-local development schemes. That is something of which the people of my constituency are well aware as are most northern Canadians. The regional development programs that have been developed particularly since the end of the Second World War will no longer be possible in their present form.
Since all Canadian producers are to some extent subsidized by government-run hydro, telephones, postal services, health care systems and so on, failing U.S. firms will never run out of grounds for filing unfair trade practice suits. Following a suit brought by the New England fishing industry, for example, the U.S. International Trade Commission identified 58, not five, not eight, but 58 Canadian government programs it labelled as unfair subsidies for the Canadian fishing industry.
That will mean that in the future, under the so-called binding dispute settlement mechanism, those same kinds of trade harassments on softwood lumber, shakes and shingles, fish, potash, pork, you name it, will still be able to proceed, and because American law prevails, the Americans will still be able to sustain the kinds of incredible harassments they have been practising against us in recent years.
A couple of areas deserve particularly close scrutiny. What about the impact on the first citizens of Canada, the aboriginal people? The only major study I have seen so far on what the impact will be on the First Nations of this country-and I do not think the Department of Indian Affairs has even touched on it-has been done by the Native Council of Canada, and it shows that the implications are devastating. This is principally because of the kinds of occupations in which most of the First Nations are still involved, including tourism, trapping and other indigenous activities including those activities in British

July 5, 1988
Canada-V.S. Free Trade Agreement
Columbia that are highly evolved in the forestry and fishing sectors. Both of those sectors, particularly in British Columbia, are under enormous threat.
What about the environment? There has been very little talk about the environment, particularly from the government side. Where is the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan)? Where has a position paper from Environment Canada been hiding, or has it been developed yet? Having studied with great care the impact of acid rain on our country, we now know that the losses in terms of tree growth is billions of dollars per year. We know that the sugar maple is dying. We know that 40,000 lakes are in the process of dying as a result of acid precipitation. Nothing is being done by the U.S. or by the present Government to deal with a very serious problem.
What is being done about the greenhouse effect? What is being done about the hole in the ionosphere caused by chlorofluorocarbons and other chemicals that have an industrial origin? These are major planetary and global matters that not only are not addressed by this deal but in fact will be made worse.
The underlying desire is to lower wage structures, to lower the availability and accessibility of social programs in order to make the systems more competitive. We must understand that in making things more profitable in the present market-driven systems we see particularly in the United States, most of the major costs are externalized. Acid rain is an externalized cost.
I was in the United States when the Hudson River caught fire. Canadians would scratch their heads and say, "Rivers catch fire in the United States?" That is how much pollution there has been on a number of occasions on the Hudson and on other rivers in the United States that they have actually caught fire from the crap floating on the surface.
What about the Niagara escarpment, the Love Canal and all of the various waste dumps there? If our industries are to be bilaterally competitive with those in the United States, will we have higher environmental standards? Do we hear the Minister of the Environment trying to sustain that argument? No, we do not, because our environmental laws will be degraded by the impact of this deal.
Let us take a contrasting look at some of the main components of Canada's economic and social system versus that of the U.S. We in Canada have universal hospital and medical coverage with compulsory employer contributions. In the U.S., 40 per cent of the population is eligible for publicly-funded hospital and medical services and 36 million Americans have no insurance. Employer contributions are voluntary. All provinces have minimum wage laws as do both territories. Nine U.S. states have no minimum wage laws, and in Texas the minimum wage is only $1.40 per hour.
In Canada we have unemployment insurance. The rate of unionization is double that in the United States. Five point 3 per cent of our national income or $3,420 U.S. per pupil is spent on education in Canada. In the U.S., it is only 3.7 per
cent of the national income. We have a much fairer system of income distribution in Canada than they have in the U.S. We know that the Canadian hospital system is the area that will first come under attack from this deal.
What do U.S. health care corporations look for when minimizing costs? In the words of a U.S. corporate executive:
You cut down on people, cut down on space, cut down wherever you can. If
you still can't solve the problem you try to find out if there are abuses.
You let some doctors go; if you feel you're doing too much indigent care you
just put a cap on the level of indigent care you will accept.
If any thinking Canadian were to take a look at what the impact on energy, the environment and social programs will be and what benefits may possibly flow from the agreement and weigh the two against each other, he or she would come to the intelligent conclusion that this deal is bad for Canada and should be opposed by every single thinking Canadian.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after all that doom and gloom, I categorically, enthusiastically support the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement because it represents significant opportunities and benefits for Canada but specifically for Alberta from where I come.
Free trade is best understood as enhanced trade, as encouraging free enterprise, as encouraging our ability to work and progress, the basis of our capitalistic, democratic society. Canada is a trading nation. The Canadian economy and society have been built and structured on foreign trade. Our ability to trade creates prosperity for Canadian families. Canada must have enhanced trade to compete in an aggressive, international market-place. Free trade means more jobs, greater job security, and lower consumer prices.
A broad spectrum of respected economic agencies promote the benefit of a secure trading market with the world's largest free enterprise economy, the United States. The agreement respects Canada's political independence and cultural sovereignty, our unique social programs and regional development policies.
At present Canada is the only major free enterprise economy that does not have unrestricted access to a market of 100 million people or more. Thus, we are economically isolated unless we trade with the U.S. For example, Israel entered into a free trade relationship with the U.S. but not with the same benefits and not as all-sweeping as ours. Israel has not lost its unique cultural or linguistic identity because of its economic trade relationship with America. The European Economic Community also expanded its market potential for Britain, France, Germany, Italy and The Netherlands. These expanded trade markets are proof that the old systems of trade protectionism must be replaced with open markets.
The free trade system will of course create significant economic benefits for Alberta's economy. Alberta will no longer rely upon domestic markets only in buying and selling
July 5, 1988

its resources. The Alberta Cattleman's Association and the Alberta Petroleum Association are avid supporters of free trade and the opportunities it will create for Albertans. An expanded and secure resource industry will create permanent service and support sector jobs.
The agreement will build a stronger future for Canada's youth. Long-term growth means existing plants must grow, and new and better facilities must open. The youth of Alberta must have the opportunity to be employed by new as well as traditional industries, or start businesses on their own. New industries will be established as a result of the agreement. Canadian industries will remain in Alberta, no longer having to relocate in the U.S. to avoid protectionist trade barriers.
Of great importance to Alberta youth are the agreement's precedent-setting arrangements regarding trade in the service sector. Alberta is world renowned for its tourist and travel opportunities as witnessed by the success of the Calgary Winter Olympics. With service sector jobs growing faster than any other sector, the agreement will ensure that opportunities abound in this area.
Most analysts agree that the free trade agreement will benefit western Canada, especially Alberta. The Canada West Foundation, a non-profit, western based research institute has done extensive research on the Alberta free trade issue. Their study confirms that free trade is beneficial for western Canada.
The agreement assures secure market access for Canadian energy exports to the U.S. Alberta oil, gas and electricity producers support the enhanced access and security to the American market and easing of National Energy Board export regulations as a positive development for the western Canadian economy.
In talking about energy we might think only of the big companies, but it involves much more than that. It affects the petrochemical industry, research, transportation by truck, rail and air, steel manufacturing, skilled trades, and construction. The service sector will expand. An increased population will result and that creates a demand for education, public services, hospital care, recreation services. All this from an expanding energy sector.
Meat packing, the largest food processing sector in western Canada, will benefit from free trade. Oilseed mills will also benefit from the removal of high U.S. tariffs on processed oilseeds. Projections indicate that the sectors directly benefiting from the agreement account for 33 per cent of Gross Provincial Product. Most important, 75 per cent of Alberta's exports depend upon a secure American market.
Again, the agreement does not and will not adversely affect existing social programs such as medicare, child care, maternity benefits, job training, pay equity, the Canada Pension Plan, pensions for the disabled, and unemployment insurance. Neither does it prevent the introduction of new programs. We must remember that all those programs must be paid for by
Message from the Senate
the Canadian people. Under the protectionist system there will be mass unemployment. We must remember that two million Canadians are working because of our exports, most of which go to the U.S.
I heard the Leader of the NDP talk about how great Canada is, and we all agree with that. He talked about the shortcomings of the Americans. After all, not every country can be as good as ours. However, essentially what he was advocating was protectionism. That is the way of the fearful. It is for those who have no self-confidence. It is for those with an inferiority complex. History has clearly demonstrated over and over again that protectionism is the way of a weak and insecure country. The NDP preach protectionism and that will lead Canada, and Alberta in particular, to stagnation, economic rust and high unemployment.
Our parents and grandparents could have said they were not going to leave the comfort of their own countries. Yet they did. They took risks, asking only for an opportunity. If this protectionist sentiment existed among our grandparents I wonder if there would have been any NDP Members here today. What if their parents or grandparents had been afraid to come to a wild country such as Canada? Wild, yes, but with opportunity.
I am suggesting that it is very important that we have this opportunity for free trade with the Americans. Theirs is the richest country in the world and they are one of the only countries who have the money to purchase some of our products and natural resources.
Several years ago we had another Government and it was supported by the NDP. Our national debt rose from SI8 billion to over $200 billion. Today we pay $29 billion in interest on that debt annually with no increase in productivity to show for it. We are now paying more in interest on that debt than we are for our social programs, and if in the last twenty years we had a Government such as this we would have been able to pay for all our social programs and we would have been eminently successful.
In conclusion, free trade offers Alberta many challenges and Canadians many opportunities. The lowering of tariff barriers and a more stable business and investment climate will stimulate economic growth and create new jobs. This will result in higher wages, an improved standard of living for Albertans, and that is why we need this agreement between the U.S. and Canada.
