subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have a few moments today, I guess 10 minutes is all I have, to speak on Bill C-130, an Act respecting free trade between Canada and the United States.
At the outset, I do not think there are too many people in the House who do not believe in improved trading relations, from wherever they may come. However, it is one thing to talk about improving our trade relations with any country and quite another to talk about jeopardizing the sovereignty of our country.
When he was campaigning for the leadership in 1983, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said, "This country could not survive with a policy of unfettered free trade. I am all in favour of eliminating unfair protectionism where it exists. This is a separate country, we'd be swamped. We have in many ways a branch plant economy, in many ways in certain important sectors. All that would happen with that kind of a concept would be the boys cranking up their plants throughout the United States in bad times and shutting their entire branch plants in Canada. It is bad enough as it is".
During that leadership campaign in June of 1983 he went on to say the following with regard to free trade, "It affects Canadian sovereignty and we will have none of it, not during leadership campaigns or any other time".
I do not think anyone could have said it better. What the Prime Minister was saying at that time was absolutely correct. It was absolutely correct in June of 1983, and it is probably even more correct in July of 1988.
In the Province of Prince Edward Island, from which I come, our most important industry is, naturally, agriculture. Our second most important industry is fisheries, and our third most important industry is tourism.
With regard to fisheries, we were told that with this Mulroney-Reagan free trade agreement we would have guaranteed and unfettered access to American markets.
Nowhere in this free trade agreement do I find that we have any protection whatsoever for our access to the United States markets as far as American remedy law is concerned, neither the laws which exist in the United States today nor the omnibus trade Bills which are before the United States Congress and the U.S. Senate at the present time.
Therefore, not only are we subjected to laws which are presently in effect in the United States, we will be further subjected to their laws in the future. There is nothing in that agreement which gives us protection from them. This agreement does not give us any more access than we have had in the past number of years. We will always be subject to American trade law.
The dispute settlement mechanism is, in my opinion, a farce. If an American manufacturer or supplier says that his product sales are being affected by subsidized goods coming in from Canada, the dispute settlement panel can only judge whether or not American trade laws have applied correctly. That is all we have, same as in the past. There is no provision whatsoever to lower the risks of such manoeuvring by American business.
On Prince Edward Island there are about 28,000 people employed, directly or indirectly, in agriculture and the fishery, that is, those involved in the processing of agricultural and fisheries products as well as the primary producers involved in the harvesting of these resources. That is about 50 per cent of our total employment force in the Province of P.E.I.
Harrison McCain is a very important business person in Atlantic Canada. Not only is McCain Foods established in Atlantic Canada but in almost every country in the world including Australia. An article in Business Watch, written by Peter Newman, quotes McCain as follows:
"We're free traders by nature," he told me. "If the government were to just come out and say, 'Hey, McCain, do you favor lowering tariffs in every case that's practical' I'd of course say 'Yes.'"
The key here is "that's practical". The article continues:
But, McCain continued, "in the case of this particular deal, I'd have to say, 'Don't dupe us in the food industry.' The problem is that we have to buy our mozzarella cheese for the pizzas we make in Canada through marketing boards. That means it costs 39 per cent more than it would in the United States. At the moment, the Americans are not allowed to ship their cheese into Canada, but with free trade, they'll be selling their pizzas here duty-free. How do we buy cheese in Canada at 39 per cent more and still be competitive? We can't be. And we have exactly the same problem with our frozen dinners because of chicken marketing boards, and so on."
That is what Harrison McCain is saying. The article continues:
"What I'd really like to hear," came McCain's parting shot, "is somebody standing up in Vancouver, or Halifax, or Toronto right now and declaring: 'Free trade is such a great deal, I'm going to start building a factory tomorrow. I'll double my capacity! I'll build a whole new industry! My God, just let me at it!' Why aren't we hearing that? I wonder ..."
A lot of Canadians are wondering that. We hear a lot from the business world in Toronto and Montreal saying what a great thing free trade is. However, I do not hear them saying
July 5, 1988

that they are going to expand tomorrow. It is not going to happen.
Returning to the fishery, a GATT ruling was imposed on fish processed in British Columbia. A fisherman by the name of Bruce Burrows wrote me an interesting letter which I want to read into the record. He said:
Before I leave to go fishing this summer I have to do a little spleen-venting about yet another example of our federal government's stupidity and spinelessness. I am referring to Brian Mulroney's decision not to contest the recent GATT ruling on exports of west coast fish.
Just to refresh your memory, this was a ruling by an international trade board, resulting from American complaints, that Canadian regulations calling for some of our fish to be processed here prior to export are contrary to the GATT Treaty.
I'll deal with the economic effects later, but the first thing that angers me about this ruling is that it's a clear violation of Canadian sovereignty. These are our fish, our natural resources. We should have the absolute and final say on how they are disposed of. If we want to rule that every salmon exported from British Columbia must have a cherry stuck in its mouth and be called a sea pig, that is our right. Our Conservative government, whose normal negotiating position in matters of American wants is either kneeling or supine with legs spread, evidently disagrees.
I think that is a good indication of the negotiations the Government has had in the past. This is not from a processor, but from a fisherman in the Province of British Columbia. He concluded:
We have, I think, only three possible courses of action-order a spine transplant for Mulroney and his cohorts, buy them all knee-pads for their next round of negotiating, or vote the mendacious sychophants out of office at the earliest opportunity.
I certainly would agree with that. The free trade agreement with which we are faced right now is certainly the most important agreement into which this country has ever entered. I believe that the people of this country must have an opportunity to express their views on it before it is passed and signed. I challenge the Prime Minister and the Government to dissolve the House immediately, to go to the electorate, and to let the people decide whether free trade is good or bad for this country. I, for one, welcome that opportunity. I would not mind coming back and supporting free trade if the people supported it. However, I can say that people from a province like mine have nothing to gain and everything to lose with free trade.
If free trade and access to the American market is such a good thing, why are the farmers, the fishermen and the forest industry in the State of Maine not making a lot of money? We know that they are far worse off than we are. They are far worse off in the hills of Kentucky than we are in this country.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the leader of the socialist Party outline the many things that make us distinctly Canadian. I support most of what he said about what makes us different, because we are different. We are Canadians.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
I differ with him in how we perceive the results for Canada if we sign a commercial trade pact with one of our trading partners. In the past 20 years, trade between Canada and the United States has increased dramatically. In that same period, many of the programs that were identified by the leader of the socialist Party were either started or improved dramatically.
We must ask, why should any further improvement or expansion of trade endanger any of those programs that we enjoy, support and that make us distinctly Canadian?
Many of the programs we enjoy require funding. The best way I know to preserve and fund those programs is to have a strong and vibrant economy.
Let me take a minute to respond to the Liberal Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) who asked a question that I believe deserves an answer. He asked why people were not standing up and announcing their plans to build plants. One reason is that his leader is entirely negative and is threatening to tear up this agreement if he becomes the Prime Minister of Canada, heaven forbid. I am sure that upon final approval of this agreement Canada will embark upon a period of stability and economic growth. This stability, in great part, will be due to the removal of the uncertainties that face our industries and traders in dealing with our largest trading partner, the United States.
I believe this arrangement will not be a disaster for Canada, nor will it be a panacea. Other problems in trade will exist, as recent rulings by GATT have shown. However, anything we can do to level the playing field for Canada is a positive step forward.
It is my intention to limit my remarks to the impact the trade deal will have on my riding, which is predominantly agricultural with a number of small industrial plants concentrated in the urban centre, as well as a single large petrochemical plant. My riding is probably not much different from many other ridings in Canada and is a fair reflection of all of Canada.
When this Government initiated the negotiations on this pact, we made certain commitments to agriculture. We promised to consult, and we did, setting up sectoral advisory groups from the private sector to assist and advise our negotiators.
The group representing basic agriculture plus the food and processing industry was made up of individuals highly respected by their peers for their experience in various sectors. Having known some of these people personally, I can assure the House that they were of the highest calibre and brought much to the bargaining table. As Canadians, we owe these people thanks for a job well done.
We also made a commitment to the supply management sector that their marketing system and the underpinnings which are necessary for it to survive, namely import controls, would remain intact. Not only did we deliver, but in the dairy sector we have added to that list a number of processed

July 5, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
products which the industry indicated were vulnerable. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has stated many times that if a secondary processed product threatens any of the supply managed systems, it will be added to the list. As well, just last week this House, under the leadership of the Government, passed in all stages a new Canada Agricultural Products Act that will protect our horticulture industry from seasonal dumping by U.S. producers.
For those who have any doubts about this Government's commitment to this sector, the Government approved the establishment of a national boiler hatching egg agency at the very time the bilateral trade negotiations were in progress.
It was our Party that established the chicken marketing agency in 1979, which the chicken producers of this country now enjoy.
Let me turn to those sectors which stand to gain by this arrangement and are supportive of the initiative. These sectors include the grains and oilseeds and the red meat groups, as well as a large number of secondary processors in the food and beverage sector.
Red meat producers have had free movement across the border with very limited tariffs for some time. Under this agreement, that access will continue.
Pork is our second largest export commodity in agriculture. We operate in what is considered to be a North American market in red meats, both cattle and hogs, where meat and meat products move back and forth across our borders with limited or no tariffs. In all cases, those tariffs are reciprocal.
Some 20 years ago, when I first became involved with the pork industry, we had 9 per cent of that North American market. Today we have 16 per cent of that market because we outsmarted and produced a better product than the Americans.
The Canadian oilseeds sector has punitive tariffs against it, which effectively has shut it out of the U.S. market. According to this agreement, those tariffs will go. End user certificates in grains will maintain our quality control system. It is a system that has made us a world leader in supplying quality grain to the export market.
According to this arrangement, the U.S. will not be able to use export subsidies for products going into the Canadian market. Canada maintains the right to protect our horticultural sector from seasonal dumping by the United States. Canadian agriculture can and will prosper.
I want to outline the benefits the trade agreement will bring to other industries in my riding. Like all other petro-chemical plants in the neighbouring riding of Sarnia-Lambton, commonly known as chemical valley, the plant in my riding is
fully supportive of the trade initiative. This plant is world scale and is looking forward to the day when the punitive tariffs against its industry will be removed.

speechtext:
The other main component of my riding affected by this deal is the small industries located in the urban centres. While some have concerns, almost without exception they believe there are opportunities.
The best way I can illustrate this is to relate what one of those small industries has done. This company previously had no involvement with the export market. When the initial announcement was made that a tentative agreement had been reached, did they cry that they would not survive? No. Did they tell their employees that their jobs would be finished? No. Did they come asking for the Government to exempt them from the deal? No. Instead, they identified their concerns, immediately hired a U.S. sales manager and participated in a major trade show for their industry in the United States.
They are convinced that they can compete. That opinion is shared by most of the other small industries in my area. In fact, most are grateful for the opportunity provided through this agreement.
We as Canadians do some things very well. Quite often we do not give ourselves credit for those things that we do so well. What has become apparent from the outset of this debate is that those people who are presently traders are fully supportive and think that this is a good deal for Canada. Those people who have never traded outside Canada have the greatest concern. I suppose that is a natural reaction, as nothing promotes uncertainty more than fear of the unknown.
I believe as Canadians that we must reject this fear. We must reject those who have no confidence in our abilities. We must take this agreement for what it is-an opportunity for our country to grow and to prosper, not only in the North American economy but in the world economy.
We can no longer hide behind the protectionist barriers of the past. We have to reach out and take our place in the world. That process begins right here with this agreement.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED

speechtext:
The House resumed from Tuesday, May 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Riis:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces in establishing a system whereby those individuals who deposit money in financial institutions not covered by deposit insurance be required to sign a waiver form indicating that they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured in the event that the institution goes bankrupt.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to this motion since I think it is an important one. If we have watched the evolution of the financial institutions in our country over the last decade then we have seen some pretty disastrous situations happen. I know that we have recognized the fact that there are certain depositors who are not protected. What we have seen as a result of the inquiry that is taking place right now in Alberta is the fact that many of these people did not realize that their deposits were not protected by insurance. Therefore, they are the ones who became innocent victims.
In this resolution what we are looking for is the ability of the federal Government to co-operate with the provinces so that there will be a consistent policy in place across the country as well as protection for those people who very often think they are protected but are not. We have grown up in a country in which there has been a great deal of trust in our banking system. Certainly, our Bank Act protects us in ways that we do not see south of the border. We now recognize that with the amendment to our Bank Act. It has allowed banks to go into the selling of securities and that type of marketing. Under the free trade agreement we no longer have the freedom to establish banking institutions in the United States. Yet the Americans can come here to establish banks because that action is not consistent with their Bank Act, whereas their banking and our selling of securities in our banks is consistent. That shows a great lack in the free trade agreement.
What we are really talking about in terms of this resolution is the fact that people who often think they are protected are not protected. As a result of the change in the Bank Act there is not the same type of protection for small investors. We certainly know that the Canadian way very often is to put the very last bit of savings that these people have into banks thinking that no matter what happens they will be protected. It seems to me it is important that we provide such protection and that it be given in consultation and through working with the provinces.
As Hon. Members know, Canadians are becoming more and more mobile. People move from one province to another. It
Financial Institutions
would be a real tragedy if there were new legislation in place which was not consistent in every province and territory. That is why the author of the resolution suggests that such a measure be undertaken with the type of co-operation that would be needed with all the provinces.
As parliamentarians we have a responsibility to look at what has been happening in our society over the last decade. We have seen some of the tragedies that have taken place. That evidence is coming out as a result of some very expensive public inquiries which have and are taking place.
My background is in prevention. When I look at public policy I like to think that we are stopping things from happening that could hurt people rather than waiting for them to happen and reacting afterwards. It is important that we look to changing the habits of investors and attempt to give them the protection that they do not now have.
As we look at this matter we see that we are not just protecting the individual as an investor but that we are protecting society collectively. Now when we get into situations where there is not this type of insurance, small business hurts. Small communities are often hurt very badly in such instances. All that is needed is the failure of one financial institution in a small community in which many small businesses have invested to see this happen.
This type of motion makes a great deal of sense to me. I hope that everyone in the House will support it. We have seen in some cases that accidents have happened, while in others we see that their cause was verging on fraudulent behaviour. This is what has been coming out of the inquiries. Unfortunately, it is always the small person who is the most vulnerable. If a person must sign a piece of paper that says that a certain amount of money is not insured and that the investment is at a greater risk, then that is very important. Very often we know that it is information that can save a great deal of heartbreak later on. That is exactly what the author of the resolution is getting at when he suggests that this become the norm for people who are participating in investment if insurance is not be in place.
We must continue to encourage people to insure the majority of their investments, particularly small investments. This would help the public, our consumers, to understand the level of risk that they are taking. It would ensure that there would be broader protection in a collective, community sense. In this way the whole financial environment could be stabilized. That is very important.
There are a great many Canadians who were shocked in the early eighties when they began to realize what could happen in the country. Up until that time we had been fairly free of that type of risk. But once the world got into financial risk situations we also became victims of it. I saw it happen in municipalities. I saw it happen with individuals. I know a great many people who thought their investments were secure and had no idea that they would suffer the losses that they did suffer.

July 5, 1988
Financial Institutions
Not only would such a measure protect the consumers, making them aware of the risks they are taking, but it would also help to give education to the consumer about the type of obligations that financial institutions are under. It would show consumers that they are not just faceless, souless types of institutions in which one puts one's money thinking it will be safe for ever and ever. It would show people that there are certain types of activities that take place that put some investments at risk. This is a good resolution.
I hope Members of the House will support the motion. I know members of my Party will support it. It is one way of helping ordinary Canadians become better informed about the type of society in which they are living, and what financial institutions can and cannot do for them. Therefore, they will be much more cautious in the investments that they make and feel much more secure about it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a strong interest in the matter raised by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). As a member of the Finance Committee I participated in our investigation into the situation of the Canadian Commercial and Northland Banks. I also participated with that committee in our study of the regulation of financial institutions. Approximately two years ago we issued a report which included major recommendations in that area. Subsequently the Government has moved in a legislative sense on most of those recommendations, not always completely in agreement, but addressing all the areas of concern.
One of the problems is that the federal Government does not have complete jurisdiction in this area. Essentially, this motion is suggesting that the Government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces. There has never been any lack of intent to co-operate with the provinces in achieving the intent of this motion. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has been attempting to do that. I suppose that is one of the difficulties of the federal system, but it is heightened in a system where people do not necessarily know under what rules the institution may be operating.
In large measure the motion has been triggered by the collapse of the Principal Group, with which I am familiar because it is resident in my own city. I might mention that none of the 127 companies associated with the Principal Group were federally registered. In fact, only one company, Principal Savings and Trust, was CDIC insured. I would suggest that if the Principal Group had been federally registered, none of those problems would have occurred, because in large measure those problems were the result of or compounded by what is referred to as "self-dealing" which are transactions between related companies. Many of those transactions would not have been allowed under the proposals put forward by the Finance Committee in the new legislation, or even under the existing legislation.
When the CCB and the Northland Bank collapsed, the federal Government paid insured depositors, as was required under the CDIC Act, and it also acted to reimburse insured depositors for two reasons. One, it felt there was an element of fairness required to reimburse those people. The Government had indicated that it wanted to see those banks continue, and that it wanted to play a part. Therefore, to some degree the Government was a partner in continuing those institutions prior to their collapse. Second, in paying out more than $1 billion to uninsured depositors, the federal Government recognized that at that time the economy of western Canada, particularly Alberta, could not stand the blow of losing $1 billion.
One of the dichotomies of this is that the Party, and the Member who proposed this motion, was one of the leading critics of the federal Government acting to reimburse a billion dollars or more of uninsured deposits. I read in an article in The Globe and Mail of March 1 that the Hon. Member is suggesting that this rule should be put in place to protect uninsured depositors, and that the CDIC Act should be amended to cover investments not backed by any form of government insurance. These include deposits of more than $60,000, foreign currency deposits, deposits with a term of maturity of more than five years, and about $3.5 billion in deposits placed with investment dealers. It behooves me to understand why day after day that Party, and the Member in particular, criticized the Government for reimbursing uninsured depositors, and now as part of this motion the Hon. Member is suggesting that it should be an every day practice.
Notwithstanding the desirability of that motion making the Government liable for every type of investment that people might make, which is obviously impractical, in a large measure we must consider that the Hon. Member is talking about areas that fall completely under provincial jurisdiction, for example, the $3.5 billion in deposits placed with investment dealers. As we know, those fall virtually under provincial jurisdiction. To suggest that the federal Government should take responsibility for insuring people who place their money with investment dealers or stockbrokers is a questionable strategy and one that I find a little strange coming from a member of the New Democratic Party.
All of us in the House believe in the concept of deposit insurance. I question that we want to insure everyone against all potential losses. The current existing deposit insurance of $60,000 protects very small investors. Those persons with greater than $60,000 in assets should have some responsibility for looking after their own affairs.
On the question of having people sign for an uninsured deposit, where the deposit is placed with what would normally be regarded as a deposit-taking institution such as a trust company, that is a reasonably and possibly effective method of consumer protection. Many of the problems that have arisen have arisen with quasi-financial institutions. The problem and the difficulty would be to define what is a legitimate deposittaking institution. Is a lawyer who receives $50,000 from each
July 5, 1988

investor and invests it a deposit-taking institution that would be drawn in under this law? Given that there is no definition or suggestion of how this might operate, we will find great difficulty in the House in accepting this motion.
In closing, the Government has been acting in the area of consumer protection. There are new measures being put forward. I agree with the Minister of State for Finance when he states that new and up-dated legislation must be brought forward. I will be supporting those Bills. I expect that the House will move on them quickly to allow the type of protection that we are all seeking. It will also prevent the type of abuses that we have seen in some of those situations.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make submissions with regard to this particular motion which states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces in establishing a system whereby those individuals who deposit money in financial institutions not covered by deposit insurance be required to sign a waiver form indicating that they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured in the event that the institution goes bankrupt.
That particular resolution has been moved by a member of the New Democratic Party. I find it somewhat curious that the New Democratic Party should move such an amendment, because it often purports to represent the ordinary Canadian, the little guy.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext: This protects ordinary Canadians.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Hear me out. The NDP has mastered the art of heckling, but I ask with respect, hear me out.
We are talking about people who deposit in excess of $60,000. I do not know about NDP Members who talk about protecting the little guy, or how much money they have stashed away, but there are not too many of my constituents in the federal riding of York South-Weston who can boast of having more than $60,000 in a bank or in a trust company, because anyone who does have under $60,000 is insured.
The NDP says that those who deposit or have on deposit more than $60,000 in a trust company or some other financial institution, a bank or whatever, should be required to sign a form that says that they are aware that their deposit is not fully insured, that the excess of over $60,000 is not insured, and in the event that the financial institution should go bankrupt, that they cannot look to the Government or to any one else for any type of compensation or recompense. It is a motherhood type of issue, but it is somewhat curious, and I found it amusing, that the New Democratic Party should be so preoccupied with protecting rich Canadians, Canadians that have more than $60,000 in the bank.
Be that as it may, I believe that no financial institution, whether it is a bank or a trust company, should ever go bankrupt if you have the proper system of regulations in place
Financial Institutions
to ensure that they do not mishandle moneys that are on deposit.
We can look at examples of banks and financial institutions that have failed-the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Those two institutions went under because you did not have the proper system, the proper laws, the proper regulations, the proper inspection in place, to ensure that they acted as trustees and that they acted in a reasonable, prudent fashion in the handling of the moneys that they were holding in trust for depositors.
I hope that a lesson was learned by the Government of Canada and, indeed, by all the provincial Governments, from one end of the country to the other, that they cannot just hope that the financial institutions will regulate themselves and will act prudently, that there is an absolute necessity that we have some very strict and stringent legislation, rules and regulations in place, with proper inspection procedures, to ensure that no bank and no trust company ever goes bankrupt. There is no reason for it. If you have the system in place, you will not have to worry about people signing waivers, people who have more than $60,000.
I know the Hon. Member from Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) is well-meaning and he is concerned about all the rich people in Kamloops-Shuswap, all those who have in excess of $60,000, but does he really believe that people going into banks really read forms? If I had the opportunity, I would put the question to him, and the Hon. Member is in the House now. Does he read every document, every form that a bank hands to him when he opens a bank account, or when he transacts business with the bank? I suspect not, because most Canadians do not. You have dozens and dozens of forms that have to be signed. Does he really believe that someone is going to be deterred-some of his rich friends on Bay Street and elsewhere-from depositing $100,000 or $150,000, or a quarter of a million dollars, because they have to sign a waiver of sorts?
I would submit that people who have that amount of money surely must be sophisticated to the point where they know that only a portion of it is insured. We are talking about people with big bucks. We are not talking about ordinary Canadians who do not have savings. They have debts.
In any event, I know that the Hon. Member is well-meaning, and he is concerned. I would submit to the Hon. Member that his efforts would be better spent, better utilized, if he were to participate with the Liberal Opposition-and hopefully members of the government side-to ensure that proper regulation and inspection, very stringent regulations, are in place to ensure that institutions do not go bankrupt.
We have a big problem, even with deposit insurance, and that is because of the terrible precedent that was set by the Conservative Government of Canada. A few years ago the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank went belly-up. They went bankrupt. All those who had $60,000 or less were reimbursed because they were insured up to that

July 5, 1988
Financial Institutions
amount. There were a great number of uninsured depositors, people that had more than $60,000. They were not insured for the portion invested that was over $60,000. The Government, in its wisdom, decided to pay off those people, those unnamed people. To this day, I do not know who those people are. I believe at the time the Government refused to submit a list. I say that they were not ordinary, poor Canadians. They were people that had substantial assets and interest.
As a result of the Government's negotiating over a billion dollars, the integrity of the system has been affected. If another financial institution goes bankrupt in the future, those people that are uninsured are going to look to the Government of Canada and they are going to cite the precedent of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank that went under during the Conservative rule of Government, in that short-lived Government between 1984 and 1988.
Regardless of the short tenure of that particular Government, the precedent was set. It was a bad move. It was an imprudent move on behalf of the Government of Canada, because it was paying off or compensating people who took risks in two financial institutions that maybe gave out more interest than a chartered bank, for example, might give on a deposit. Those people who take those risks have to be prepared to pay the price, in the event that, statistically, they are caught in the remote situation where a financial institution goes bankrupt. Where the Government went wrong is that it compensated those people. In effect it set a precedent.
In closing let me say that the resolution does not do any harm. It is motherhood in nature but, as I indicated earlier, I am surprised at the concern of the Hon. Member from Kamloops-Shuswap about his rich friends on Bay Street, those who have more than $60,000. It does not do any harm to co-operate with the provinces and have the people sign one extra form to say that, in the event that the institution goes bankrupt, they cannot hold anyone responsible. I reiterate that a more comprehensive approach ought to be taken. Unfortunately, the NDP at times look at problems in a very narrow, simplistic fashion. If they do not like the banks, nationalize the banks, they say, in their policy platform. If they do not like cable companies, nationalize them. In terms of the problem before us, and that is the trust in banks and financial institutions, a comprehensive approach is necessary to ensure that laws are in place here in the Parliament of Canada, in each of the legislatures across the country, to make sure that these financial institutions are properly controlled, properly monitored, so you do not have a situation where these institutions go bankrupt. Thank you, Madam Speaker, for giving me the chance to say a few words on this subject.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) which says, and I quote:
... the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces in establishing a system whereby those individuals who deposit money in financial institutions not covered by deposit insurance be required to sign a waiver form indicating that they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured in the event that the institution goes bankrupt.
As many of my colleagues did earlier in this debate, I would like to start by thanking the House Leader of the New Democratic Party for giving us this opportunity in the House to address the matter of protecting consumers of financial services in Canada.
I am sure Hon. Members will agree that financial institutions should provide their customers with more information about the deposit insurance available to them.
As you know, a great deal has already been done in this respect, and I am thinking of the reform of our financial institutions, and the federal Government has initiated various attempts in this direction in connection with its responsibility for the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, and I am referring more specifically to Bill C-42, legislation that reinforces federal supervision of financial institutions. Watchdog agencies will be regrouped in the new Office of the Superintendant of Financial Institutions. Thanks to the new powers conferred on it by this legislation, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will be in a better position to protect the interests of depositors and other creditors. Federal regulators will also have more definite and more specific powers that allow them to take over financial institutions that are insolvent or have failed to meet their legal obligations.
At the present time, the Government is committed to reinforcing its ability to supervise financial institutions as part of a comprehensive reform of the financial sector. Formerly, four federal agencies were involved in a supervisory role. The Office of the Inspector General of Banks supervised chartered banks; the Department of Insurance supervised insurance companies and federally-chartered trust and loan companies; the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation insures deposits and the Bank of Canada plays the role of lender of last resort. The other important measures contained in the bill are the consolidation of the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and of the Department of Insurance into a new Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, and some provisions would amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act.
Thus, any unauthorized statement by agents of a member institution of the CDIC that their institution or its deposits are insured is prohibited. Secondly, any member institution that takes an uninsured deposit must provide written notice of that fact on the deposit receipt, and member institutions that solicit funds for investments for a person who is not a member of the CDIC have an obligation to advise their clients of the fact that such investments are not insured.
Furthermore, the Government is considering new measures to protect consumers in light of the growth of one-stop shopping for financial products. These measures will aim to ensure that consumers are informed, firstly, of the identity of the person they are really dealing with when they purchase
July 5, 1988

financial products or services sold by a financial institution, and secondly, of whether their deposits or investments are insured or not.
All federally-regulated financial institutions, including banks and insurance conpanies, trust companies and lending institutions with federal charters, will be governed by these new measures.
The motion, seen in the context of Government policy, proposes the selection of a specific provision in the overall context of the implementation of Government strategy. Like most of the Members who took part in this debate, I feel that this or a similar measure certainty deserves to be examined by the officials of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
However, I must point out that the measure proposed in the motion raises a number of questions. It overlooks the fact that we do not realty have a single deposit insurance system. In fact, our system here in Canada consists of a number of insurance plans covering deposits and similar investments held by financial institutions. These deposits may be insured under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, but also the Regie de Vassurance-depot du Quebec which, like the CDIC, insures deposits with loan and trust companies and credit unions chartered by the Province of Quebec; by the Corporation de fonds de securite of the Desjardins Group, which also covers credit unions in Quebec; by various stabilization funds and deposit insurance companies that provide a similar service for credit unions in the other provinces; and by compensation plans for holders of life insurance and general insurance annuities and policies. Deposit insurance plans vary, depending on the institutions-banks, credit unions, insurance companies, and so forth-and the federal or provincial authorities responsible for their charter.
When the motion refers to insured deposits, it is therefore not immediately clear what is meant. And it is not a foregone conclusion that the proposed measure is the best way to ensure that consumers receive all the information they need. The motion also suggests co-operating with the provinces. That is not a problem, because since 1984, this Government has promoted co-operation and reconciliation with the provinces, and we have proved that we can agree and enter into agreements with the provinces. Nevertheless, we must not forget that these institutions are federally chartered and are thus supervised by the federal Government.
For these reasons I cannot support the motion in its present form. With my other colleagues, however, I want to join the House Leader of the New Democratic Party in asking the authorities responsible for various deposit insurance plans at both levels of government to set a priority on implementing measures that will improve consumer access to information on deposit insurance.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad to speak on this important subject. We have now spent just half
Financial Institutions
our allotted time on this motion and it is the fourth time the motion has been called for debate. I hope our time is being used well. Certainty Members on this side of the House have been making effective contributions to our understanding of the basic issues which underlie this motion.
Let me go over what we understand the key issue to be. We do not believe that the issue is the form of consumer protection, that is, the precise mechanics and wording of the regulations. We believe that the real issue is the fact of consumer protection; the concrete steps already taken by our Government to ensure that legitimate rights of depositors are effectively secured. Financial issues, with implications for consumer protection, have been raised in this House many times in the past. We are all well aware of the kinds of problems that have arisen and might conceivably arise again. I do not suppose any Member in this House is not aware of some of the dimensions of the problems.
But when I turn from the underlying situation and the very real issues which can be discussed to the particular motion we are debating this afternoon, I begin to have certain problems. Let me go over them. First, this motion raises the subject of consumer protection and, of course, that is well done. But it assumes that the Government has not already acted effectively through legislation and regulation. The motion ignores the further measures to protect consumer interests that will be an important part of further legislation to reform the financial sector.
Finally, the motion makes a single proposal as if that measure, and that measure alone, were a perfect and sufficient solution to the problems. I happen to believe that we can agree on a goal of consumer protection without accepting the rightness of this particular solution.
While I have no problem with the Hon. Member's choosing to raise the issue in this House, I do have difficulties with his tactics and with his motion. As I have said, it is important to be aware of the concrete steps taken by the Government to overcome problems in the system. While I am satisfied that a good system is in place already, I would certainty agree that if improvements can be made, they should be made. Let me go over the provisions of the present system so that all Hon. Members are clear on what is happening already.
Our financial sector reform to date has involved two Bills passed and proclaimed last summer. Even before the Government moved on these two Bills, however, non-members of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation were prohibited from representing themselves as being insured by the CDIC. For some time, there has been a requirement that uninsured instruments should be stamped as such.
As I understand it, some people have from time to time had problems with institutions falsely claiming coverage or falsely claiming that specific instruments were covered. That is a problem with all regulation. We cannot regulate against

July 5, 1988
Financial Institutions
misrepresentation, whether it is intended or not. If the existing provisions of the law have been ignored, that is not in itself an argument for adding to the regulations, the tack being taken by those who support this motion. Rather, it is justification for more stringent administration of the regulations, such as that which has been encouraged in our reforms of the financial sector.
Bills C-42 and C-56 which implemented the first stages of that reform included both general and specific measures relating to consumer protection. Together they established a more effective supervisory authority. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions replaces the former Inspector General of Banks and the Superintendent of Insurance, and the new office has been given greater powers and resources to ensure that its duties are well carried out.
In addition, this stage of the reform strengthened the CDIC. As a result, that corporation is better able to carry out its own functions. Together, this means that the kinds of situations which have arisen in the past, in part perhaps as the result of overstretched supervisors without the resources or powers needed, will not happen again.
Bill C-42 also added three further important elements to the existing CDIC regime. First, it made clear that the existing ban on unauthorized representations of insured status of member institutions or deposits received by them applies both to the institution and to all persons acting as their agents.
Second, the Bill made it a statutory requirement that when an institution takes a deposit which is not insured, this must be indicated in writing on the deposit contract. This provision comes very close to the proposal made by the motion before us, and the change made in Bill C-42 moves it from the regulations to the law itself.
Third, Bill C-42 instituted a new requirement that institutions that solicit funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or other non-members of the CDIC must give notice to investors that these companies are non-members and that such funds are not insured by the CDIC.
I have already mentioned that the Government will be proceeding as quickly as possible with the remaining legislation to implement its reform of the financial sector. Among other things, those proposals will grant broader in-house powers to federal financial institutions to enable them to provide their clients with a wider range of financial services.
Specifically, financial institutions will be permitted to own or to enter into networking arrangements with other types of financial institutions. We expect that this will provide Canadians with more choice and more convenience in obtaining the financial services they want. As well, the diversification of institutions into new lines of business should enhance their ability to meet the challenge of increasing competitiveness, both domestic and international.
A number of consumer protection issues arise, of course, in this new situation. For example, insured deposit-taking services may be only one of the services offered by a group of related financial institutions, not all of which are members of the CDIC. The draft trust and loans legislation takes account of this by enabling the Governor in Council to make regulations imposing terms and conditions on the activities that companies undertake in the areas which will be open to them. Similar provisions will be incorporated in the legislation governing banks and insurance companies. Although there will be a more complex situation than at present, we have already taken steps to ensure that consumers are protected.
Bill C-56 also dealt with certain aspects of this general problem. Some of its provisions will facilitate the creation of annuity and policy-holder compensation plans. The final details are still being worked out, but these plans will fill a gap in the insurance of deposit-like instruments. They will extend a form of coverage for insurance company annuities similar to that which the CDIC provides for deposits.
Work is already taking place to implement the measures set out in Bill C-42. The CDIC is always vigilant to ensure that it takes account of concerns expressed by others, especially Members of this House, and that it considers changing circumstances as well.
I am satisfied that a good system is being put in place, and I believe this motion ought not to be accepted as it stands. It does not recognize the many measures now in place. Nonetheless, I hope we will see the degree of co-operation the Hon. Member wants and that this country will continue to enjoy a financial system that protects the interests of all involved.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today's debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) gives me a welcome opportunity to address a number of concerns about consumer protection in the financial system. I know these concerns are common to many Members on both sides of the House. I think it is particularly appropriate to be looking at the consumer protection issues raised in this motion at a time when other consumer protection issues in the sector are also in the news.
Hon. Members opposite, or alongside of me in the House, and I share concerns in this case, but I have to be frank and make it clear that our common goals do not mean that we agree on the motion. Indeed, we approach this motion in very different ways.
Earlier in the debate when the motion first came before the House, I heard it being used as a springboard from which to attack the Government for its position with respect to the Principal Group's activities rather than as a means of discussing the most effective way to secure protection for the interests of consumers. That was disappointing, both because it diffused attention that should be paid to the issue of consumer protection and because it showed that this motion's mover either did
July 5, 1988

not know or did not care about the jurisdictional limits on the federal Government's role in the financial system.
Having said this, I want to return to the important issues raised by this motion. Events of past years have ensured that we are all very sensitive to situations in which it appears that additional measures or actions are needed to protect the interests of consumers, depositors and others. We must always be vigilant, we must always have concern for the legitimate interests of the people who use our financial system. As a Government, we have already moved to make significant changes in the former regime to do just that.
To set the scene, I want to remind Hon. Members that even under the former regime, the law prohibited any institution other than a member of the CDIC from representing itself as a member of the CDIC. Then in Bill C-42, proclaimed last July, the Government undertook a number of specific improvements to the CDIC regime. It made three specific improvements to the provisions about which the Hon. Member is concerned. We have now entrenched in legislation regulations which ensure that when institutions take deposits which are not insured, they must indicate that in writing on the contract.
Second, we have extended the ban on unauthorized representations of the insured status of institutions or deposits to persons acting as agents for institutions.
Third, we have also required that member institutions soliciting funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or other non-members of CDIC must give notice to potential investors that these funds are not insured by CDIC.
The CDIC covers all federally regulated deposit taking institutions and the major provincially regulated deposit taking institutions as well. It seems to me that for companies within federal jurisdiction our measures go almost as far as the Hon. Member's motion if we assume that people signing contracts read them. That is surely not an unreasonable assumption to make when we are drafting laws and regulations. As a result, I think the legislation and regulations which govern these institutions is already in an acceptable state.
The motion before us draws attention to institutions and other types of instruments other than classic deposits. Many of these other institutions and instruments are already being used. As the Government's reform of the financial sector continues to be implemented and as the sector grows accustomed to the new opportunities it has, we can expect even more options and new developments. That means that it will be increasingly important to pay attention to consumer protection. For example, the new networking proposals which will undoubtedly give new opportunities to institutions and new options to their customers will also mean that customers will need more knowledge of these institutions. We have already seen links growing between banks which are members of the
Financial Institutions
CDIC and security dealers which are not. Our reforms will now permit even further linkages.
At the same time, in order to deal with legitimate concerns, our reforms lay out requirements for organization, for corporate and individual behaviour, and for disclosure which will provide a significant increase in consumer protection. I hope that the legislation on trust and loan companies will soon be before us. In the meantime, we have been assured that the remaining legislation to implement reform will follow the outlines of the draft released in December, 1987. On that basis the Government is clearly moving effectively to deal with potential problems.
However, the legislation, when considered and passed into law by Parliament, will give the Government the power to make regulations imposing terms and conditions with respect to the potentially confusing activities of member institutions which are linked to non-members and which offer a variety of services, some of which are insured deposits and some of which are investments.
I think it is appropriate that the Government is also working with the insurance industry to arrive at an acceptable way of dealing with some deposit-like instruments. In effect, we want to find a way of insuring CDIC-like coverage for policy holders in both sectors of the industry. I understand that the two plans, one for the life and health companies and one for the property and casualty companies, should be in operation by the end of 1988 or the beginning of 1989.
I want to congratulate the Government, and particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), on their concern for consumer protection in the financial sector. Their actions and proposals enhance disclosure. They strengthen the regulatory and supervisory authorities. They have added significantly to the requirements of the CDIC. They ensure that those who take reasonable care and are not the objects of deliberately misleading activities will have the proper information and can make decisions without confusion.
No doubt there can be improvements. I do not know of a perfect system anyway. However, I do not think there is the kind of urgency for further change that lies behind Motion M-143. We are after all looking at an evolving system where many new provisions have to be allowed to settle down. It would in my opinion be premature to mandate further changes at this time, especially when, as I pointed out, the substance of the Hon. Member's proposal has already been effectively incorporated in changes made last year by this House.
